meta.title: Who really said "Before you speak, listen. Before you write, think. Before you spend, earn. Before you invest, investigate. Before you criticize, wait. Before you pray, forgive. Before you quit, try"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Shakespeare never wrote it. William Arthur Ward published these lines in his 1968 book Thoughts of a Christian Optimist; the Bard got the credit by 2010.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Before you speak, listen. Before you write, think. Before you spend, earn. Before you invest, investigate. Before you criticize, wait. Before you pray, forgive. Before you quit, try'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator traces the passage to William Arthur Ward's 1968 Thoughts of a Christian Optimist. Shakespeare was handed the credit by 2010.

answer.label: Not Shakespeare — actually William Arthur Ward
answer.sourceLine: Shakespeare never wrote this. The lines are William Arthur Ward’s, published in his 1968 book Thoughts of a Christian Optimist, and Quote Investigator ↗ finds the passage was “implausibly reassigned” to Shakespeare by 2010. The version that travels under Shakespeare’s name is not an excerpt of Ward but a rewrite of him: it keeps five of his nine lines, drops three, adds two he never wrote, and turns his closing “Before you die, give” into “Before you die, live.”

source.excerpt: Before you speak, listen. Before you write, think. Before you spend, earn. Before you invest, investigate. Before you criticize, wait. Before you pray, forgive. Before you quit, try. Before you retire, save. Before you die, give.
trail: 1907 — one line is already loose in the world. Quote Investigator ↗ traces “Before you invest, investigate” to Rex Beach’s article “The Madmen of the Desert” in The Saturday Evening Post, 13 July 1907, in a passage about Nevada mining investment.

1968 — the passage reaches print, credited. William Arthur Ward publishes all nine lines in Thoughts of a Christian Optimist, catalogued as Droke House, Anderson S.C., 1968, 89 pp., LCCN 68013823 ↗. QI credits Ward with the aggregation while noting some lines already circulated. Quote: The Weekly Digest reprints it that November with acknowledgement.

1974 — the byline falls off. The compilation 1800 Quips for Speakers and Writers reprints the passage under the label “Excellent advice:” but without attribution ↗. Copies circulating without Ward’s name are free to drift, and QI records that the passage was later modified and supplemented.

1977 — the name is still there. Lloyd Cory’s compilation Quote Unquote prints the passage on page 254 credited to “William A. Ward” ↗. The 1974 anonymous printing did not erase the byline permanently — attribution ran intermittently, which is how a line can be both properly credited and quietly orphaned at the same time.

By 2010 — Shakespeare collects. QI’s verdict is that the passage was “implausibly reassigned to William Shakespeare” ↗. Corrections followed quickly: “No, that’s William Arthur Ward” ↗, one debunking blog answered, printing the full nine lines.
source.cutTag: Bold — the three lines the Shakespeare version drops
source.excerptNote: Ward’s list runs nine lines. The version that circulates under Shakespeare’s name is not a shortened Ward but a rewritten one. The Shakespeare-attributed text Quote Investigator reproduces ↗, posted to a Google Group in September 2010, reads: “Before you speak »Listen / Before you write »Think / Before you spend »Earn / Before you pray »Forgive / Before you hurt »Feel / Before you hate »Love / Before you quit »Try / Before you die »Live.” Five of Ward’s lines survive intact; three — invest, criticize, retire — are gone; two are lines Ward never wrote; and his closing give has become live. QI’s own summary of the mutation: the passage “was later modified, supplemented, and reassigned to William Shakespeare.”

source.rightsNote: These lines are not public domain. They were first published in Ward’s Thoughts of a Christian Optimist in 1968 — well after the 1931 threshold — and US works published between 1964 and 1977 with a copyright notice received automatic renewal, giving them a 95-year term that runs into the 2060s. Who holds those rights today is not publicly recorded: the book was published by Droke House (Anderson, S.C.), and no renewal or assignment record we can cite says whether the copyright stayed with the publisher or with Ward — so for permission, start with the publisher or Ward’s estate. The Shakespeare misattribution is doubly costly here: it strips a modern author’s estate of credit and falsely implies the text is ancient and free to use. (The one exception is “Before you invest, investigate,” which per Quote Investigator was already in print in 1907 and is old enough to be public domain on its own.)

author.name: William Arthur Ward
author.kicker: The man who actually wrote it
author.heading: William Arthur Ward, the most-quoted writer nobody can name
author.bio: William Arthur Ward (1921–1994) was an American motivational writer who produced more than 4,000 epigrams — short, balanced, aphoristic lines built for greeting cards, church bulletins, and desk plaques. His sayings ran in Reader’s Digest and in his “Pertinent Proverbs” column for the Fort Worth Star-Telegram, and were collected into some thirteen books. Ward spent his working life in Texas as a public-relations man and educator, serving for decades as assistant to the president of Texas Wesleyan College. His fate is a peculiar one: he is quoted constantly and credited rarely — which is precisely how a famous name ends up on his work.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and who earned it
misattribution.intro: This is a twentieth-century American epigram wearing an Elizabethan coat. The misattribution is recent, traceable, and — on the evidence — entirely groundless.

items.why: There is no evidence he wrote any of it. Quote Investigator ↗ dates the reassignment to no later than 2010 and calls it implausible. The passage is absent from Wikiquote’s list of quotes misattributed to Shakespeare, and the Folger Shakespeare Library’s roundup of fake Bard quotes doesn’t cover this one either — but the Folger does warn that “fake Shakespeare quotes are being shared on social media” ↗ every day.

Ward gathered this line rather than coining it. QI traces it to Rex Beach ↗, in his article “The Madmen of the Desert” in The Saturday Evening Post of 13 July 1907, written about Nevada mining investment — sixty-one years before Ward’s book. QI credits Ward with the aggregation, noting some lines were already in circulation.

items.scope: Extra lines in longer online versions
items.why: The passage didn’t just change hands, it changed shape. QI records that it was modified and supplemented ↗ before and during its Shakespeare phase, so circulating copies may carry lines Ward never wrote alongside ones he did.

items.scope: The passage printed with no author at all
items.why: By 1974 the compilation 1800 Quips for Speakers and Writers reprinted the passage without attribution ↗, even though Quote: The Weekly Digest had credited Ward properly in November 1968. An orphaned quote is a quote waiting for a famous name.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator ↗ credits the passage to William Arthur Ward and his 1968 book Thoughts of a Christian Optimist, finding that it was “implausibly reassigned to William Shakespeare by 2010.”

context.heading: Why this one travels so well
lead: The passage is engineered to spread. Nine imperatives, each an identical two-beat snap — before you X, Y — with no clause longer than four words. It is the prose equivalent of a drumbeat, and it was built that way on purpose: William Arthur Ward wrote epigrams the way other people write jingles, for greeting cards and newspaper columns where a line has about one second to land.

But the very quality that makes it memorable is what strips it of its author. A line this compact needs no context, so it gets copied without any — and an orphaned aphorism drifts until it finds a famous name to attach to. Shakespeare is the strongest gravitational field in the English language. The odd part isn’t that the passage ended up under his name; it’s that anyone believed it, given how modern Ward’s counsel sounds. Not the words themselves — retire, save and invest were all available to Shakespeare, and he used them. It’s the senses: retire meaning to leave the workforce on a pension, and invest/investigate as personal financial advice, belong to a twentieth-century idiom. The vocabulary is Elizabethan; the meanings are not.
context.detailsSummary: The mechanism: how a credited quote becomes an anonymous one
detailsBody: Quote Investigator's citation trail shows the attribution being sanded off in stages rather than in one dramatic act. The passage appeared in Ward's 1968 book, and was printed in Quote: The Weekly Digest in November 1968 with acknowledgement. By 1974 it was reprinted in the compilation 1800 Quips for Speakers and Writers without attribution — though three years later Lloyd Cory's Quote Unquote (1977) still credited “William A. Ward” on page 254.

So the byline didn't snap off once and for all; it flickered. That is the more ordinary way attribution dies — not one dramatic theft but a compilation here printing the name and a compilation there dropping it, until enough nameless copies are in circulation that the nameless version becomes the default. A quotation anthology that drops the byline converts a sourced line into a free-floating one, and every copier downstream of it inherits the anonymity rather than the citation. Decades of that, and the internet supplied a name — the biggest one available.

There is a further wrinkle that argues against Shakespeare on internal evidence alone. Ward's list did not spring fully formed from his own head either: QI traces “Before you invest, investigate” to Rex Beach in 1907, writing about Nevada mining swindles. Ward's achievement was the aggregation — gathering and shaping existing counsel into a single cadenced sequence. That is a real authorial act, and it happened in 1968, not 1600.
context.pull: Ward is quoted constantly and credited rarely. That gap is exactly where misattribution grows.
